name: The Packet Rats
motto: If it moves through wire, we see it.
description:
The Packet Rats are a crew of fifteen data thieves operating out of a decommissioned telecom switching station in Gary, Indiana — a location chosen specifically because Gary's infrastructure is so degraded that nobody monitors it, but its fiber trunk lines still connect to the GLMZ's main data backbone. The Rats tap into those trunk lines and siphon data like mosquitoes on an artery. Corporate communications, financial transactions, personal messages, logistics manifests — anything that passes through unencrypted or weakly encrypted channels, the Rats capture, sort, and sell.

The crew is young — average age twenty-three — and almost entirely self-taught. They grew up in the net, learned to code before they learned to fight, and view physical reality as an inconvenient obstacle between them and the data streams they live in. Several members run neural interfaces that keep them jacked in nearly twenty hours a day, which is doing visible damage to their health and social skills but makes them extraordinarily fast in digital space. They can crack mid-tier encryption in minutes, spoof corporate authentication protocols, and navigate network architecture that would baffle a legitimate security team.

What the Packet Rats lack is physical capability. They're hackers, not fighters. Their switching station has a single reinforced door and a handful of scavenged weapons that most of the crew barely know how to use. They survive by being hard to find, by being useful to people who are dangerous, and by having enough dirt on enough people that eliminating them would trigger a catastrophic data dump. The dead man's switch is their best defense — a distributed system that will broadcast their entire stolen archive if the crew goes dark for more than 48 hours.
ideology: Information wants to be free — and expensive. The Packet Rats believe that data hoarding by corporations is a form of tyranny, which conveniently aligns with their business model of stealing and selling that data. There's genuine anti-corporate sentiment mixed in with the profit motive, but the profit motive is winning.
territory: A decommissioned telecom switching station in Gary, Indiana. Their operational reach extends across the GLMZ's data infrastructure.
methods: Trunk line tapping — physical splices into fiber optic backbone lines running through Gary
Traffic interception — automated systems that capture, filter, and categorize intercepted data
Encryption cracking — neural-interface-assisted decryption of mid-tier corporate communications
Data brokering — selling intercepted intelligence to buyers across the GLMZ
Dead man's switch — a distributed failsafe that dumps their entire archive if they're eliminated
Social engineering — using stolen data to manipulate, blackmail, or impersonate targets
resources: Physical access to GLMZ fiber optic trunk lines
Custom interception and filtering hardware built into the switching station
Neural interfaces optimized for sustained network immersion
An archive of intercepted data spanning years of corporate and personal communications
The dead man's switch — mutually assured destruction as a defense strategy
Relationships with buyers who value their product: syndicates, fixers, journalists, rival corporations
story_hooks: The Rats intercepted something that got one of their members killed — now they need protection while they figure out what it means
A corporation has located the switching station and is sending a team — the Rats need to evacuate or be destroyed
The dead man's switch malfunctioned and a partial data dump has already started — the Rats need it stopped before the full archive goes public
A Rat is selling data to both sides of a syndicate war, and when it's discovered, the whole crew becomes a target
The Rats found evidence of a corporate atrocity in intercepted communications and are debating whether to release it or sell it
